description: We are tackling the Flame in Freefall challenge by focusing on microgravity fire safety, life-critical systems architecture, and OT risk mitigation. Our project combines combustion telemetry analysis, ICS/SCADA security, predictive hazard models, and fail-safe override protocols.
summary:
Fire behaves differently in microgravity: without buoyant convection, smoke lingers near its source and standard ceiling detectors fail. Flame in Freefall uses NASA’s open BASS-II data, 129 real microgravity burn trials, to better understand and predict fire risk in space habitats.

We engineered combustion metrics (oxygen depletion, CO₂ and carbon monoxide production) and trained two Random Forest models: an ignition classifier (76% accuracy on held-out trials) and a carbon monoxide severity regressor (57.5 ppm mean absolute error). We then modeled the detection pipeline as an ICS/SCADA system with four risk tiers (NOMINAL, WATCH, WARNING, CRITICAL), 2-of-3 sensor voting, signed commands, and a hash-chained audit log to defend against sensor spoofing and other OT cyberattacks.

The result is a proof-of-concept, security-conscious blueprint for automated fire safety on long-duration missions, where crews can’t rely on ground support.
details:
What it does and how it works

Flame in Freefall turns NASA’s microgravity combustion data into a fire-risk prediction and a secure response design for space habitats. We used the 129 burn trials in NASA’s BASS-II investigation (PSI-25). For each trial we computed oxygen depletion, CO₂ production, and carbon monoxide production, plus a fuel-material category. We then trained two Random Forest models: an ignition classifier (76% accuracy on 33 held-out trials) and a CO severity regressor (57.5 ppm mean absolute error). A rule-based risk engine turns the model output into four tiers (NOMINAL, WATCH, WARNING, CRITICAL). Only the highest tier triggers automatic containment, and lower tiers alert the crew or raise monitoring.

Cybersecurity layer

We modeled the pipeline as an ICS/SCADA system with field sensors, an edge controller, a supervisory dashboard, and actuators. We designed 2-of-3 sensor voting so one faulty or spoofed sensor can’t trigger a shutdown. Our threat model covers six scenarios (sensor spoofing, command injection, denial of service, firmware tampering, replay, and log tampering). Each is mapped to a defense, such as signed commands, a fail-safe watchdog, and a hash-chained audit log.

Benefits and intended impact

Standard ceiling smoke detectors rely on gravity-driven airflow, so they fail in microgravity. This project gives a data-grounded starting point for early, automated, tamper-resistant fire protection on long-duration missions, where crews can’t depend on ground support.

Tools used

Python, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, Matplotlib, Jupyter notebooks, and GitHub. The data came from NASA’s open Physical Sciences Informatics repository.

What is creative

We combined two areas that are usually separate: combustion-risk machine learning and operational-technology security. The AI’s output is treated as a safety-critical signal that has to be protected, not just a prediction.

Factors we considered

  • Small data: 129 trials is a small dataset, so we report results as they are.
  • Proxy labels: NASA provides no ground-truth hazard label, so our ignition flag and CO-rise severity are derived proxies.
  • Missing time-series files: The BASS-II table has before/after measurements rather than time-series traces. NASA’s Saffire-I telemetry files were also unavailable because of broken storage links.
  • False alarms: We balanced automatic response speed against the cost of an unnecessary suppression discharge.

This is a proof-of-concept. The ICS/SCADA layer is a documented design with a working risk-engine implementation. We did not build or deploy hardware.
